stemMd: Officials in a school district want to find out whether using a new reading app for $20$ minutes a day improves the reading scores of the district's fourth-grade students. Which study design would best allow the officials to conclude that using the app causes an improvement in reading scores for all fourth-grade students in the district?

options.label: A
options.textMd: Select $200$ of the district's fourth graders at random and have all $200$ use the app daily for one term. Compare their reading scores at the end of the term with their scores at the start.

options.label: B
options.textMd: Select $200$ of the district's fourth graders at random. Ask which of them already use the app at home, and compare the reading scores of the users with those of the non-users.

options.label: C
options.textMd: Take all the fourth graders at the two schools whose principals volunteered. Randomly assign half of them to use the app daily for one term and the other half to follow the usual routine. Compare the two groups' changes in reading scores.

options.label: D
options.textMd: Select $200$ of the district's fourth graders at random. Randomly assign $100$ of them to use the app daily for one term and the other $100$ to follow the usual routine. Compare the two groups' changes in reading scores.

explanationMd:
A conclusion of the form "the app causes an improvement for all fourth graders in the district" makes two claims, and the design has to support both.

- **Cause.** The study needs a comparison group and random assignment to it. Random assignment makes the app group and the comparison group alike, on average, in everything except the app, so a difference in score changes can be credited to the app.
- **All fourth graders in the district.** The participants need to be a random sample of the district's fourth graders, so that they represent that population.

Only one design does both: select $200$ fourth graders at random from the whole district, then randomly split them into an app group and a usual-routine group and compare the score changes.

The other designs each lose one of the two claims.

- Having all $200$ randomly selected students use the app and comparing end-of-term scores with start-of-term scores has no comparison group. Fourth graders' reading scores rise over a term anyway, through ordinary teaching and growth, so a rise cannot be credited to the app.
- Comparing students who already use the app at home with those who do not is observational. Families who chose the app may read more at home or care more about reading, and that, not the app, could explain the difference.
- Randomly assigning the app within two volunteering schools does support a causal claim, but only for students like those in those two schools. Schools whose principals volunteer may differ from the rest of the district, so the result cannot be generalised to all the district's fourth graders.

distractorRationale.a: The students are a random sample, but there is no comparison group. Reading scores normally rise over a term, so a before-and-after gain cannot be attributed to the app.
distractorRationale.b: This is an observational comparison. The students chose whether to use the app, and families who use it may differ in other ways, such as how much they read at home, that also affect scores.
distractorRationale.c: Random assignment supports a causal claim, but only for students like those at the two volunteering schools. Those schools were not randomly chosen, so the result cannot be generalised to the whole district.

accessibilityText: A school district wants to know whether using a new reading app for 20 minutes a day improves reading scores of its fourth graders. Which study design best supports concluding that the app causes improvement for all fourth graders in the district? The choices are: select 200 of the district's fourth graders at random and have all of them use the app daily for a term, comparing end-of-term scores with start-of-term scores; select 200 of the district's fourth graders at random, then randomly assign 100 to use the app daily for a term and 100 to follow the usual routine, comparing the two groups' score changes; select 200 of the district's fourth graders at random, ask which already use the app at home, and compare the reading scores of users and non-users; take all fourth graders at the two schools whose principals volunteered, randomly assign half to use the app daily for a term and half to the usual routine, and compare the score changes.

provenance.notes: Original item. Asks for the design that supports both a causal claim and generalisation to a population; each distractor removes exactly one requirement (control group, random assignment, or random selection).

independentSolve.workingNotes: Needs both random sampling from all district fourth graders (to generalise) and random assignment (for causation); only D has both. A has no control group, B is observational, C uses volunteer schools so cannot generalise to the whole district. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave8-sat-math-run1) reached the same answer: Needs both random selection from district fourth graders (generalise) and random assignment (causation): only D. A has no control group; B is observational; C uses volunteer schools, so not generalisable to the district.]
